content: National guidelines for the effective management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) should be developed in collaboration with local experts in STI management, public health, and laboratory sciences. Phased Approach to STI Guideline Development: 1. Phase 1 (November 2013 – April 2016): This phase focuses on treatment recommendations for specific STIs, including Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea), HSV-2 (genital herpes), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). It also includes syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women. Independent modules will be developed for these infections. Additionally, guidelines for syndromic STI management and a clinical management package will be created. 2. Phase 2 (2017 – 2018): This phase emphasizes STI prevention strategies, including the use of condoms, behavior change communication, biomedical interventions, and vaccines. 3. Phase 3 (2017 – 2018): This phase addresses the treatment of additional infections not covered in Phase 1, such as Trichomonas vaginalis (trichomoniasis), bacterial vaginosis, Candida albicans (candidiasis), Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis), human papillomavirus (HPV; genital warts/cervical cancer), Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies), and Pthirus pubis (pubic lice). 4. Phase 4 (2017 – 2018): This phase focuses on laboratory diagnosis and screening for STIs. The independent modules from Phases 1 and 2 will later be consolidated into a single comprehensive WHO guideline for STI case management. Overview of Genital Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Guidelines: Epidemiology and Burden: HSV-2 is the leading cause of genital ulcers globally, with approximately 19.2 million new infections among individuals aged 15–49 in 2012. An estimated 417 million people were living with HSV-2 in the same year. HSV-1, traditionally associated with oral herpes, is increasingly recognized as a cause of genital herpes, particularly in high-income countries. HSV-2 is of particular concern due to its strong association with HIV transmission, as individuals with HSV-2 are three times more likely to acquire HIV. Clinical Presentation: HSV-2 infection often causes recurrent genital ulcer disease (GUD). While most initial infections are asymptomatic or atypical, symptomatic cases may present with painful genital lesions, itching, dysuria, and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Recurrent episodes are typically less severe but can cause significant physical and psychological morbidity. Laboratory Diagnosis: Diagnosis of genital HSV infection often requires laboratory testing to differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2. Methods include antigen detection, viral culture, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), and serological assays for type-specific antibodies. Rationale for Updated Recommendations: The 2003 WHO guidelines for genital HSV treatment need updating to address the evolving epidemiology of HSV-2 and its interaction with HIV. Recommendations for acyclovir treatment, including optimal dosing and duration, are essential, particularly for immunocompromised individuals and those living with HIV. Suppressive therapy has been shown to reduce both HSV-2 and HIV viral shedding and recurrence. Objectives of the Guidelines: To provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of genital HSV infection. To support countries in updating their national guidelines for managing genital HSV. Target Audience: These guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels, including those involved in sexual and reproductive health programs, such as HIV/AIDS, family planning, and maternal and child health. They are also relevant for policymakers, program managers, and other professionals responsible for implementing STI management interventions. Structure of the Guidelines: The guidelines include evidence-based treatment recommendations for common clinical conditions caused by genital HSV infection. They also provide direction for countries to adapt these recommendations based on local antimicrobial resistance patterns, healthcare capacity, and resources. Dissemination and Implementation: The guidelines will be made available as printed publications, online downloads, and through WHO’s Reproductive Health Library. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating recommendations will be established within a year of implementation. Conclusion: The WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital HSV infection aim to provide the best global evidence for managing this condition while allowing for local adaptation based on epidemiological and healthcare factors.
